messages.subject: Summary: power function for hypotheses from regression models
messages.subject_clean: Summary: power function for hypotheses from regression models
messages.body_plain:
Hi all

Admittedly after only one day, I have received no responses to my query on
power functions for hypotheses from regressions (see below for initial
query).  However, I was in a bit of a rush and only needed something rough,
so when I saw the solution offered at
http://mercury.bio.uaf.edu/~biolwild.organizations/courses/97wlf625/guide.ht
m I knocked up the following single line of code without really stopping to
think too deeply about it even though it seemed way too simple to be true...
It certainly came up with answers that look plausible, so I tentatively
offer it for others' criticism, advice that I am completely out to lunch, or
edification.

cheers
PE

reg.power <- function(b, se, alpha=0.05)
{
# computes rough estimate of power from regression for parameter
# with true value b and standard error se, with null hypothesis b=0.
#
pnorm(qnorm(alpha/2) - b/se) + pnorm(b/se - qnorm(1-alpha/2))
}

Suggested usage, for (as an example) a regression coefficient with an
estimated standard error of 0.2 is:

plot(-100:100/100, reg.power(-100:100/100, 0.2), type="l",
ylab="Power", xlab="True value of parameter",
main="Power of two-tailed test")

> -----Original Message-----
> How can one go about calculating the power function for a particular
> hypothesis from a regression model or (better still) a binary family GLM?
> eg I am interested in the power of the test
>
> Hnull: B7=0 versus
> Halt:  B7 != 0
>
> where B7 is one parameter in the linear predictor.  The predictor variable
> it is the coefficient of happens to be a dummy variable, if that makes any
> difference...
>
> Any references or S+ tips greatly appreciated.
>

messages.subject_clean: Summary: power function for hypotheses from regression models
messages.body_plain:
On Fri, 1 Jun 2001, Peter Ellis wrote:

> Hi all
>
> Admittedly after only one day, I have received no responses to my query on
> power functions for hypotheses from regressions (see below for initial
> query).  However, I was in a bit of a rush and only needed something rough,
> so when I saw the solution offered at
> http://mercury.bio.uaf.edu/~biolwild.organizations/courses/97wlf625/guide.ht
> m I knocked up the following single line of code without really stopping to
> think too deeply about it even though it seemed way too simple to be true...
> It certainly came up with answers that look plausible, so I tentatively
> offer it for others' criticism, advice that I am completely out to lunch, or
> edification.

For least-squares regression it is a standard calculation.  Assuming
normality, the t-ratio (betahat_i - beta_i)/s sqrt((X'X)^{-1}_{ii}) has a
non-central t distribution, and you can get the power from pf (as S+3.4
at least does not handle non-central t distributions).  For generally,
pf can be used to give you the power of any F test of a subset of the
coefficients being zero.

For a binary family GLM it is much harder.  First, which test?
The Wald test of the coefficient and the likelihood ratio test can be
quite different.  For neither is there any exact distribution theory
that I know of.  Asymptotics are not going to give a good enough
answer in general for large departures from the null (especially for the
Wald test).

>
> cheers
> PE
>
> reg.power <- function(b, se, alpha=0.05)

messages.body_plain:
Professor Ripley

Many thanks for your reply.

> For least-squares regression it is a standard calculation.  Assuming
> normality, the t-ratio (betahat_i - beta_i)/s sqrt((X'X)^{-1}_{ii}) has a
> non-central t distribution, and you can get the power from pf (as S+3.4
> at least does not handle non-central t distributions).  For generally,
> pf can be used to give you the power of any F test of a subset of the
> coefficients being zero.

Thanks for the pointer; from the pf help file I now see that this would
imply:

reg.power2 <- function(b, se, alpha=0.05, df1=1, df2)
{
1-pf(qf(1-alpha,df1,df2), df1, df2, (b/se)^2)
}

which is asymptotically the same as my first effort, but better for smaller
samples.

The more difficult question of applying to a GLM will have to wait; an OLS
answer is good enough for my (very) rough purposes at the moment.

PE

messages.subject: Re: bias-corrected boostrapped confidence bound for correlation
messages.subject_clean: bias-corrected boostrapped confidence bound for correlation
messages.body_plain:
Jae Lee asked:

>Does anyone have a S+ function to obtain
>bias-corrected bootstrapped confidence bounds
>for correlation coefficient?

limits.bca() does BC intervals if you set acceleration=0.
By default it estimates acceleration and calculates BCa intervals.

# Example:
X _ rmvnorm(15, d=2)
bootResults _ bootstrap(X, cor(X)[1,2])
limits.bca(bootResults)  # BCa interval
limits.bca(bootResults, acceleration=0) # BC interval

tree using just one row, S-Plus crashes.

So, for example,

or

tree (Kyphosis ~ ., data = kyphosis[1,])

both cause S-Plus to crash. I admit this doesn't come up much (it arose here
inside a call to edit.tree(), in fact), but surely there ought to be a saner
response than a crash -- right?

Sam Buttrey

messages.subject: Problem specifying time zone
messages.body_plain:
Here is a little script that creates some timeDate objects, t1, t2, and t3.

The character strings giving the date and time are identical, except 
that t1 is in so-called "daylight savings time" (PDT, pacific 
daylight time) and t2 and t3 is in standard time (PST, pacific 
standard time). Two different values for the zone argument of 
timeDate() are used.

By definition,
  PST is 8 hours behind GMT
  PDT is 7 hours behind GMT

As can be seen in the output below, Splus ignores the time zone given 
in the character string, and in the case of t3 ignores the zone 
argument given to timeDate() and treats them all as PDT.

Yes, I know that 6/1/2001 is in fact a date from PDT. None the less, 
the supplied zone information is ignored.

This looks like a bug to me.
I need a way to persuade Splus that the data really is what it says it is.

I am receiving data from a measurement device that, for whatever 
reason, always reports in PST, regardless of the date. For example, 
an event that takes place at 16:00 PDT is reported as taking place at 
15:00 PST, which is perhaps unconventional, but correct. I wish they 
would report it in GMT, but they don't.

Thanks
-Don

t1 <- timeDate('6/1/2001 1:00 (PDT)',format="%m-%d-%02y 
%H:%02M",zone='PST/PDT')

cat('t1: ',t1 at time.zone,t1,'\n')

t1 at time.zone <- 'GMT'

cat('t1: ',t1 at time.zone,t1,'\n')

t2 <- timeDate('6/1/2001 1:00 (PST)',format="%m-%d-%02y 
%H:%02M",zone='PST/PDT')

cat('t2: ',t2 at time.zone,t2,'\n')

t2 at time.zone <- 'GMT'

cat('t2: ',t2 at time.zone,t2,'\n')

t3 <- timeDate('6/1/2001 1:00 (PST)',format="%m-%d-%02y %H:%02M",zone='PST')
cat('t3: ',t3 at time.zone,t3,'\n')
t3 at time.zone <- 'GMT'
cat('t3: ',t3 at time.zone,t3,'\n')

cat('t1, t2 identical?',all.equal(t1,t2),'\n')
cat('t1, t3 identical?',all.equal(t1,t3),'\n')

>  source('tst.sp')
t1:  PST/PDT 6-1-01 1:00
t1:  GMT 6-1-01 8:00
t2:  PST/PDT 6-1-01 1:00
t2:  GMT 6-1-01 8:00
t3:  PST 6-1-01 1:00
t3:  GMT 6-1-01 8:00
t1, t2 identical? TRUE
t1, t3 identical? TRUE

(And please comments from non-Americans about our bizarre and 
misnamed "daylight savings time". I too think it's a crock.)

--

--------------------------------------

Don MacQueen

Environmental Protection Department

Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory

Livermore, CA, USA

--------------------------------------

messages.subject: Predicteds for negative binomial - wrong scale?
messages.subject_clean: Predicteds for negative binomial - wrong scale?
messages.body_plain:
Dear listers. (S-PLUS 2000, Intel, Win98SE)
I'm doing regression for count data. Getting predicted values from a 
poisson model is straightforward. When I fit the same data to a negative 
binomial model, the predicted values are on some other scale. The 
coefficients are nearly exactly equal between the models. From the poisson 
model, predict.glm with type="response" gives values that I expect. From 
the negative binomial model, predict.glm with type="response" gives values 
that are way too high. However, if I use predict.glm with type="link", the 
values are what I expect, i.e. equal to the ones from the poisson model.

Running the same models in Stata 6.0, there is no such problem. The values 
on the original scale (type="response") and also the linear prediction 
(type="link") are the same between models and plausible. The commands are 
"predict var, n" equivalently to type="response" and "predict var, xb" 
equivalently to type="link".

Since we are going to publish this, I just want to check that this is 
indeed expected behaviour. That the coefficients are equal I know is a 
feature of our data, not the methods in general. The standard errors are 
different, though. Why is this phenomen happening ? How do you interpret 
predict with type="response" from a negative binomial model ?

The following S+ code reproduces the code.
> library(mass)
> poisson <- glm(count ~ time, data = oslo, family = poisson)
> negbin <- glm.nb(count ~ time, data = oslo)
> coef(poisson)
 (Intercept)       time
   0.1406699 0.2401174
> coef(negbin)
 (Intercept)       time
   0.1406698 0.2401175
> poisson.pred <- expand.grid(time = c(1, 2))
> poisson.pred <- cbind(poisson.pred, response = predict.glm(poisson, 
predict, type = "response"))
> print(poisson.pred)
     time response
1   1      1.151045
2   2      1.463436

## These values are too high:#########
> negbin.pred <- expand.grid(time = c(1, 2))
> negbin.pred <- cbind(negbin.pred, response = predict.glm(negbin, predict, 
type =  "response"))
> print(predict)
     time response
1   1      3.161493
2   2     4.320781

## These values are OK: #########
> negbin.pred <- expand.grid(time = c(1,2))
> negbin.pred <- cbind(negbin.pred, response = predict.glm(negbin, predict, 
type =  "link"))
     time response
1   1      1.151045
2   2      1.463436

I'm grateful for any help.
Yours, Jan Brogger, University of Bergen, Norway

[1] 3.161495 4.320780

messages.subject: problem passing arguments in integrate()
messages.body_plain:
i think this a question about passing arguments and not about integration
but you can be the judge of that.

help for the integrate function gives an example of a double integral:

# Example 3:  A double integral demo to evaluate the
# double integral: integral(0,5) integral(0,t) f(x) dx dt
# where f(x) is x^2.  Result should be 5^4/12, or 52.08333.

double.integral.demo.fn <-
function()
{
        fun <- function(upper, integrand)
        {
                unlist(lapply(upper, function(upper, integrand)
                {
                        integrate(f = integrand,
                                  lower = 0,
                                  upper = upper)$integral
                }
                , integrand))
        }
        return(integrate(f = fun,
                         lower = 0,
                         upper = 5,
                         integrand = function(x)
                                        {
                                                x^2
                                        }
                )$integral)
}

it is passing the integrand as an inline function integrand=function{x^2}
which is a function of x only.  cute trick:)

if the integrand is really a function of both x and t how could it be
passed?

as an example, use 2*(t^2)*exp(x*t) just to be a pain.

integral(0,5) integral(0,t) 2*(t^2)*exp(x*t) dx dt = 

integral(0,5) 2*t*exp(t^2) dt =

exp(25) - 1

if you can't integrate non-separable functions of two variables, is there a
trick for integrating separable functions of two variables?  by separable i
mean f(x,y) = g(x)*h(y).

thanks
bob

messages.subject: Re: Problem specifying time zone
messages.body_plain:
Short answer:

Before doing your time calculations, run the
commands

> timeZoneList("PST" = timeZoneC("st/pacific"))
> timeZoneList("PDT" = timeZoneC("st/mountain"))

Now try your time string.  (S-PLUS does not use any
time zone info found in a time string.  Zone info
must be given to the "zone = " argument.  You
could parse this time zone info out of the 
string if needed.)

> timestring <- '6/1/2001 1:00 (PST)'

> tt <- timeDate(timestring,
+                in.format = "%m/%d/%Y %H:%M (%03Z)",
+                zone = "PST",
+                format = "%m/%d/%Y %02H:%02M:%02S:%03N %Z"
+                )
> ttPSTPDT <- tt
> ttPSTPDT at time.zone = "PST/PDT"
> 
> tt
[1] 6/1/2001 01:00:00:000 PST
> ttPSTPDT
[1] 6/1/2001 02:00:00:000 PST/PDT
> 
> 
> ttPST <- tt
> ttPST at time.zone = "PST"
> ttPDT <- tt
> ttPDT at time.zone = "PDT"
> 
> ttPST
[1] 6/1/2001 01:00:00:000 PST
> ttPDT
[1] 6/1/2001 02:00:00:000 PDT
> 

This should give you the right times for
the machine that always puts out PST
(i.e. minus 8 hours from GMT).

Note the "in.format" I use above in the
timeDate() command.  I had
problems parsing the time string with
round brackets surrounding the time zone.

(I'm using
> version
Version 6.0.1 Release Candidate 2 for Microsoft Windows : 2001 

but this should work for any Unix/Windows S-PLUS version with the new
timeDate functions and objects.)

Gory details:

Ah, the fun we have with time and calendars!
The concepts seem clear enough, but start
looking closely, and things begin to slip
through your fingers.  A year - what is that?
One trip around the sun?  How long does that
take?  The definition of a year took centuries
to get a grip on.  Days and weeks were "disappeared"
by popes and other high magnates, in a
concerted effort to bring this unruly beast
under human control.  Then Einstein came along,
and I don't even want to get started on what
that guy did to time!

Sorry for the digression, but the marking of
time is a fascinating human endeavor.

The new timeDate() function in S-PLUS is a
great addition to the time series function
base, and once the kinks are smoothed out
and quirks of time understood this function
makes life a lot easier.

The new built-in time zone class objects
are all listed on the help page for
"class.timeZone"
(Due to bugs in the RC2 help system, you will
 need to type in
 class.timeZone
 in the Search tab window of the help system,
 click the List Topics button, then select
 the "time Zone Classes" entry that shows in the
 topics list below, to get this help page.)

st/mountain is 7 hours behind GMT permanently.
st/pacific is 8 hours behind GMT permanently.
us/pacific has daylight savings time adjustments
built in.

Unfortunately all three time zone definitions
"PST", "PDT", and "PST/PDT" in the
timeZoneList() definitions are all associated
with the "us/pacific" built-in object.

It would be better for some purposes to have
"PST" associated with "st/pacific" and
"PDT" associated with "st/mountain"
so that PST is always 8 hours behind GMT and
PDT is always 7 hours behind GMT.  

This can be accomplished by using
timeZoneList("PST" = timeZoneC("st/pacific"))
timeZoneList("PDT" = timeZoneC("st/mountain"))

(Whether or not it is a bug that S-PLUS does not
use this definition is endlessly
debateable, and no doubt will be, just as people
debated the date of the True Third Millenium over
the last couple of years; Jan 1, 2000 or
Jan 1, 2001?  Slippery indeed.
In my opinion, you are right, and PST and PDT
should be defined as above.)

The zone that gets specified as a string in timeDate()
calculations must be the name of a list element returned
using the 
timeZoneList()
function.  This function reports the state of
the global variable ".time.zone.list".
This list has named list elements, and it is
these list element names that must appear
in the zone =  argument to the timeDate()
function or for the time.zone slot of timeDate
objects.  When you start S-PLUS, this
".time.zone.list" object is in the "splus"
database.  (Use the command 
> find(".time.zone.list")
to find out where this list is in your search path.)

If you use the timeZoneList() command to respecify
any time zone info, a new copy of ".time.zone.list"
is placed in frame 0, the session frame,
so will be present until you quit S-PLUS.
(If you want these definitions to always
be available, you can put the timeZoneList()
commands 
timeZoneList("PST" = timeZoneC("st/pacific"))
timeZoneList("PDT" = timeZoneC("st/mountain"))
in your .First file.)

Here is a listing of the time zone list elements,
after specifying the commands

> timeZoneList("PST" = timeZoneC("st/pacific"))
> timeZoneList("PDT" = timeZoneC("st/mountain"))

messages.subject: Re: Problem specifying time zone
messages.body_plain:
In my reply to Don MacQueen's query about timeDate objects,
I erroneously stated that S-PLUS ignores time zone information
contained in a time text string.

S-PLUS DOES consider the time zone portion of the string
as this example indicates:

> timeZoneList("PST" = timeZoneC("st/pacific"))
> timeZoneList("PDT" = timeZoneC("st/mountain"))
> 
> x <- timeDate(c("June 1, 1998 2:04 PM (PDT)",
+                 "June 1, 1998 2:04 PM (PST)"),
+                 in.format = "[%m %d[,] %Y] %H:%02M %p (%3Z)",
+                 format = "%m/%d/%04Y %H:%02M %p (%Z)",
+                 zone = "PST/PDT")
> x
[1] 6/1/1998 14:04 PM (PST/PDT) 6/1/1998 15:04 PM (PST/PDT)
> 

My apologies for this error.

Be aware that the time string parsing does not warn
the user of illegal times such as

April 1, 2001 2:04 AM (PST/PDT)

> x <- timeDate(c("April 1, 2001 2:04 AM (PST/PDT)"),
+                 in.format = "[%m %d[,] %Y] %H:%02M %p (%7Z)",
+                 format = "%m/%d/%04Y %H:%02M %p (%Z)",
+                 zone = "PST/PDT")
> x
[1] 4/1/2001 1:04 AM (PST/PDT)

S-PLUS decides that 2:04 AM PST/PDT is after the
daylight savings time switch, so adds 7 hours instead of 8,
yielding the GMT time

> y <- x
> y at time.zone = "GMT"
> y
[1] 4/1/2001 9:04 AM (GMT)

but 4/1/2001 9:04 AM (GMT) is really
4/1/2001 1:04 AM (PST/PDT)

This does appear to be a bug, and I will
report it.

Steven McKinney

messages.subject: Odd problem
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

 I'm having this odd problem where I take some data out of a table,
multiply it together and get the *wrong* answer.

 If I do it semi-manually, using the same formula I get the right answer.

 I've checked it and re-checked it but I can't see what's going wrong.

 I'm hoping someone can spot the error. (My system is Splus 2000 r3 on 
win98).

Here's the code, part .1. is just setting up the data and I don't
think the problem occurs there.

# .1. setting up data
set.seed(1)
x<-c(rep(0,500),rep(1,500))
p<-exp(.1-.8*x)/(1+exp(.1-.8*x))
y<-matrix(0,1000,1)
for (i in 1:1000) {y[i]<-sample(c(0,1),1,prob=c(1-p[i],p[i]))}
y.df<-data.frame(y=y,x=x)
# end setting up data

# .2. problem starts
y.tab<-table(y.df$x,y.df$y)
a<-y.tab[1,1]
b<-y.tab[1,2]
cc<-y.tab[2,1]
d<-y.tab[2,2]
# the formula mk I
(a+cc)*(b+d)*(a+b)*(cc+d)
#I get wrong answer: [1] 1470457856
# a+b and cc+d both equal 500 so the above is obviously wrong.

#what the data looks like
y.tab
a
#I get 243
b
#I get 257
cc
#I get 317
d
#I get 183

#manually assign the values
a<-243
b<-257
cc<-317
d<-183
# the formula mk II
(a+cc)*(b+d)*(a+b)*(cc+d)
#I get right answer: [1] 6.16e+010
#

Ta,
Megan Pledger

accessing individual data in any sheet of an excel file, I learned the
following:

worksheets inside a loop.

messages.subject: Re: Odd problem
messages.body_plain:
The problem here is integer overflow.  On Windows, the maximum value of an
S-PLUS integer is:

> .Machine$integer.max
[1] 2147483647

In S-PLUS 2000, the table function returns values stored as integers.  The
objects a,cc,b,d are therefore all integers, and the value of the
calculation

> (a+cc)*(b+d)*(a+b)*(cc+d)

overflows the maximum integer value, and S-PLUS returns nonsense.

So why does it work when you enter the calculation by hand, I hear you ask?
In S-PLUS 2000 (in fact, and Sv3 based version of S-PLUS), whenever I type
an expression like:

> 560*440*500*500
[1] 6.16e+10

The terms of the expression (560, 440, 500, 500) are all coerced to double
precision floating point before the calculation is made.  You can see this
by using storage.mode on a literal number:

> storage.mode(560)
[1] "double"

The calculation is done in double precision floating point, whose maximum
represented value is:

> .Machine$double.xmax
[1] 1.797693e+308

The result of the calculation fits well within this value.

Now, in Sv4 based versions of S-PLUS (i.e. S-PLUS 6 for Windows and Unix),
things change a little.  S-PLUS 6 does not coerce literal integers to double
precision in arithmetic:

S6> storage.mode(560)
[1] "integer"

So this situation arises more often than in S-PLUS 2000 (where integers were
rare, unless you were trying hard to make them, or using a few particular
functions -- like table).  Fortunately though, S-PLUS 6 detects integer
overflow and returns an NA instead:

S6> 560*440*500*500
[1] NA

Incidentally, this is a potential source of difference when running a script
written for Sv3 under Sv4, but it was felt better to keep literal integers
as integers (and return NA in overflow cases) rather than coercing
everything to double as S+2000 did.

Hope this clears up the mystery!

# David

> > x*y*(z^2)
> [1] 6.16e+10
>
> I find the last line particularly intriguing....

Unlike the arithmetic operators +, -, *, and %/% which return integer values
for integer operands, the operators ^ and / always return double precision
results, regardless of the storage modes of the operands.

For all operators, if any one operand is double precision, the calculation
and the result are double precision too.  That's why x*y*(z^2) returns the
correct double-precision result, and why also

> 560*440*500*500.
[1] 6.16e+010

gives the right answer.  Note the decimal point at the end: 500. is a
literal double precision value.

# David

When mode(x) is "numeric", the data of
       x may be stored as integers,  or  as  single-precision  or

For many years, Fortran programmers have written numbers like

100.0d0

to ensure that a value was stored as double-precision and not integer or 
single precision.  It seems that it is time to bring to S+ the practice of 
always writing floating-point numbers with a decimal point.

What I wonder about, though, is how S+ decides whether to store as single 
or double precision!  That choice could be quite important as a problem 
progresses.

Incidentally, I dislike relying on implicit type conversions in any 
language. They prove to be made as one would wish about 99.9% of the time, 
which of course leads to a finite number of avoidable errors.

1) The panel strip label across the top of each panel is black,
and hides the text label for that panel. How do I make it white,
so that my labels show through?

2) The dots that represent the data points are open. How do I
make them solid black?

3) I'd like to plot a loess line in each panel. There's an example
of how to do this on p. 280 of the Programmer's Guide. When I try
to apply that example to my situation, I get an error message that
says something like "Argument y not matched: ", and then a string
of numbers that are the values of YEAR, each replicated four times.
Presumably, there's something I need to do first, or something I
need to add to the function call as given in the manual to get it
to work. Does anybody know what that might be?

I received replies from Nick Ellis, Naomi Robbins, Jason Connor, and
Dennis J. Murphy. I'm grateful for the replies I received, and was able
to get a graph that's very close to what I want using the following:

strip.background <- trellis.par.get("strip.background")
strip.background$col <- 0
trellis.par.set("strip.background", strip.background)
strip.shingle <- trellis.par.get("strip.shingle")
strip.shingle$col <- 0
trellis.par.set("strip.shingle", strip.shingle)
sym <- trellis.par.get("plot.symbol")
sym$pch <- 16
trellis.par.set("plot.symbol",sym)
xyplot(SKR ~ YEAR |BASETMTF, data = Skr1, as.table = TRUE, strip =
function(...) strip.default(...,strip.names = c(T,T)), panel=function(x,y)
+ {panel.xyplot(x,y);  sub <- !is.na(x) & !is.na(y);
+ panel.loess(x[sub],y[sub], span=1)})

However, now that the strip backgrounds are not obscuring the strip
labels, I can see that the strips are being labeled with the numeric
value of the grouping variable BASETMTF, rather than the actual factor
levels. In other words,

> levels(Skr1$BASETMTF)

yields

[1] "Control" "B"       "D/D"     "B/D/D"

but the strip labels are simply "1", "2", "3", and "4". However, the
section "Changing the text in strip labels" on p. 376 of the Programmer's
Guide implies that the output of levels() is exactly what should appear
in the strip labels. What am I doing wrong now?

regards,
Mark A.

Hello everyone,

 

I found this useful mailing list yesterday. 

 

I have a question whose answer I can't find in the book 
neither on the Mass help. I will try to be very precise and descriptive so that 
you can give a very short answer without losing much time with 
this.

 

I am currently modelling a data set whose response variable 
consist of a three-classed [0,1,2] wild pigs abundance. I did a polytomous 
logistic regression (PLR) with a variable forward selection. If we read 
McCullagh&Nelder as well as Hosmer&Lemershow we see that in 
the PLR with a p-classed response variable, the outputs would consist in (p-1) 
models, one for each logit.

The 'polr' funcion output consists of unique 
values for the estimated parameters with different intercepts as shown 
below:

Intercepts:

      Value Std. Error 
t value 

0|1 
-4.5220  1.9488    -2.3204

1|2 
-1.4923  1.8739    -0.7964

Does this mean that the adjusted models are two parallel lines 
where the two logits would differ only in the intercept?

 

Also the 0|1 and 1|2 confuses me. According to 
Hosmer&Lemershow the first logit would compare category 0 with category 1 
and the second logit would compare category 0 with category 2. Does it work in 
the same manner with 'polr'? Or is the second logit comparing category 1 with

messages.subject: Re: Odd problem
messages.body_plain:
Andrzej Tadeusz Galecki <agalecki at umich.edu> writes:

>  For many years, Fortran programmers have written numbers like
>  
>  100.0d0
>  
>  to ensure that a value was stored as double-precision and not integer or 
>  single precision.  It seems that it is time to bring to S+ the practice of 
>  always writing floating-point numbers with a decimal point.
>  
>  What I wonder about, though, is how S+ decides whether to store as single 
>  or double precision!  That choice could be quite important as a problem 
>  progresses.

>  Incidentally, I dislike relying on implicit type conversions in any 
>  language. They prove to be made as one would wish about 99.9% of the time, 
>  which of course leads to a finite number of avoidable errors.

I couldn't agree less!!!  The beauty (one of the many beauties) of
S is that the user does ***not*** have to jack around with type
declarations (and dimensioning, and various other administrative/
bookkeeping details) but is free to concentrate on substance.

We may be asking a bit much of S(plus) to do ``type conversions'';
there are too many conflicting desiderata.  Wouldn't it be better
to leave the storage mode as double for ***all*** numbers?  This
has, I guess, the impact of fuzzifying such expressions as ``a==b'',
but we've been living with this for years, and coping.

On this theme, I must admit I don't understand what Prof. Ripley
wrote earlier:

>> What I wonder about, though, is how S+ decides whether to store as single
>> or double precision!  That choice could be quite important as a problem
>> progresses.

> It doesn't, AFAIK.  It always uses double unless the user specifies
> otherwise (via storage.mode<- or as.single).  Some older compiled code does
> use single precision internally.

But in Splus 5.x and higher we get

S+5.1 > storage.mode(500)
[1] "integer"

for example --- which is basically what started this thread.  There
must be some distinction that I'm not making, but I don't get it.
Could Prof. Ripley (or somebody) please enlighten my feeble mind?

                                        cheers,

                                                Rolf Turner
                                                rolf at math.unb.ca

messages.body_plain:
On Wed, 6 Jun 2001, Rolf Turner wrote:

> On this theme, I must admit I don't understand what Prof. Ripley
> wrote earlier:
>
> >> What I wonder about, though, is how S+ decides whether to store as single
> >> or double precision!  That choice could be quite important as a problem
> >> progresses.
>
> > It doesn't, AFAIK.  It always uses double unless the user specifies
> > otherwise (via storage.mode<- or as.single).  Some older compiled code does
> > use single precision internally.
>
> But in Splus 5.x and higher we get
>
> S+5.1 > storage.mode(500)
> [1] "integer"
>
> for example --- which is basically what started this thread.  There
> must be some distinction that I'm not making, but I don't get it.
> Could Prof. Ripley (or somebody) please enlighten my feeble mind?

Ah, he asked `store as single or double precision', thereby excluding
integer, and I answered the exact question.

As for integer, it varies by version:

In S3, essentially 1:n was integer, everything else double.
In S4, integers parsed as integers are stored as integer.  Anything
parsed as a double us stored as a double.

In both, calculations entirely in integers result in an integer, but
others (including exponentiation) switch to double.

Hope that helps as a broad brush: There are a few exceptions (such as
factor codes).

--

Yesterday I asked why the strips in an xyplot were being
labeled with factor numeric values (1 through 4), rather
than with the names of the factor levels (which, in this
case, are "Control", "B", "D/D", and "B/D/D"). I have
received two reponses so far.

1) Nick Ellis says:
>Hmm. I don't reproduce your code's behaviour. Try this
>
>strip.background <- trellis.par.get("strip.background")
>strip.background$col <- 0
>trellis.par.set("strip.background", strip.background)
>strip.shingle <- trellis.par.get("strip.shingle")
>strip.shingle$col <- 0
>trellis.par.set("strip.shingle", strip.shingle)
>sym <- trellis.par.get("plot.symbol")
>sym$pch <- 16
>trellis.par.set("plot.symbol",sym)
>new.iris <- as.data.frame.array(iris, col.dims = 2)
>names(new.iris) <- make.names(names(new.iris))
>xyplot(Sepal.W. ~ Sepal.L. | species, new.iris,  as.table = TRUE, strip =
>function(...) strip.default(...,strip.names = c(T,T)), panel=function(x,y)
> {panel.xyplot(x,y);  sub <- !is.na(x) & !is.na(y);
> panel.loess(x[sub],y[sub], span=1)})
>
>I see labels "species: Setosa" etc.
>
>I'm using Splus 2000 release 2.

Submitting the above gets me a blank graph sheet and
"Error: Object "species" not found". I'm using S-PLUS
2000 Professional Release 1 under Windows 98.

2) Steven Riley says:

>I haven't used the xyplot function much but I did encounter the same
problem
>as you are experiencing with the strip labels at one time.  I managed to
get
>the strip labels I wanted using the following approach:
>
>x<-levels(Skr1$BASETMTF)<-c("Control","B","D/D","B/D/D")
>
>for (i in 1:length(x))
>{
>xyplot(SKR ~ YEAR |x[i], data = Skr1, as.table = TRUE, strip =
>function(...) strip.default(...,strip.names = c(T,T)), panel=function(x,y)
>+ {panel.xyplot(x,y);  sub <- !is.na(x) & !is.na(y);
>+ panel.loess(x[sub],y[sub], span=1)})
>}
>
>I cannot remember if I had to mess with anything else in the xyplot command
>but you may be able to give this approach a try.  Good luck!

Submitted as is, the above gives me a blank graph sheet. If I take out
the "for" loop and change the xyplot call to xyplot(SKR ~ YEAR | x, etc.),
S-PLUS opens a graph sheet, plots a single point, and stops, with the error
message "Error in .C("loess_raw",: span too small.  fewer data values
than degrees of freedom."

Right now, my inclination is to just let this one go, and explain the
numeric labels in the figure legend, unless I can figure out an approach
that works. Factors just seem more and more like a bad idea all the time
to me.

regards,

Venables and Ripley (p.263, 3rd ed.) include a direct function
minimization method which can be faster and more reliable than EM. 

If you still want EM, the following is an EM mixture of normals based on 
Hamilton's book "Time Series."

I haven't looked at this for some time so I don't recall
all the details.  But in any case, the Hamilton reference
plus this code may be helpful to you.  In addition to 
implementing what Hamilton describes, this also includes
a wrapper function that allows you to call the base
function multiple times with different starting points. 

matt kurbat

------------------------------------------------

############################################################################
##
#
#       FUNCTION:
#                       simulateMON
#       PURPOSE:
#                       Generate a sample from a mixture of normals
distribution
# 
#       INPUTS:
#                       SampleSize      Size of simulated data sample to be
generated
#
#                       MONparams               Mixture parameter vector
(p,u1,u2,s1,s2)
#       OUTPUT:
#                       SimdMONdata     Simulated mixed normal data
#
simulateMON<-function(MONparams,SampleSize)
{
        x<-rnorm(SampleSize,MONparams[2],MONparams[4]) # Generate sample
from first normal dist
        y<-rnorm(SampleSize,MONparams[3],MONparams[5]) # Generate sample
from second normal dist.
   a<-rbinom(SampleSize,1,MONparams[1])                         # Generate
SampleSize Bernoulli r.v.'s with success prob=p. 
   SimdMONdata<-a*x+(1-a)*y                                     # Linear
combination that generates sample ...
        
# ... from mixture distribution g.  
}
#
####### END OF FUNCTION "simulateMON"
########################################

#######  FUNCTION EMmon
#########################################################
#
# FUNCTION:
#               EMmon
#
# PURPOSE:
#               ESTIMATES PARAMETERS FOR A MIXTURE OF N NORMALS FOR A DATA
VECTOR.
#
# REFERENCE:
#               SEE HAMILTON, JAMES D.(1994).  TIME SERIES, PP.685-689.
#
# RECOMMENDATION FOR CHOOSING INPUT PARAMETER VALUES:
#               * "MaxNumEMiterations" SHOULD BE CHOSEN SO THAT ALGORITHM
CONVERGES
#                       MOST BUT NOT ALL OF THE TIME.
#
# INPUTS:
#               "InitialMONparams"              
#                                               MIXTURE OF NORMALS (MON)
PARAMETERS.
#                                               THESE MUST BE INPUT IN THE
ORDER
#
InitialMONparams=(p1,p2,..p(N-1),u1,u2,...,uN,s1,s2,..,sN) 
# <FUTURE - CONVERT TO P1-PN INPUT - DO GlobalOptEMmon SIMULATANEOUSLY>
# 
#               "InputData"                             
#                                               A DATA VECTOR
#
#               "MaxNumEMiterations"                    
#                                               MAXIMUM NUMBER OF ITERATIONS
OF THE EM ALGORITHM
#                                               FOR MON TO OBTAIN
CONVERGENCE.  THIS MAXIMUM NUMBER
#                                               IS OVERRIDDEN IF ERROR
TOLERANCE "EMprecis" (NEXT
#                                               ARGUMENT) IS SATISFIED.  
#
#               "EMprecis"      
#                                               PRECISION REQUIRED FOR
CONVERGENCE OF EM ALGORITHM
#
#               "NumNormals"                            
#                                               NUMBER OF NORMALS IN THE
MIXTURE OF NORMALS
#
# OUTPUTS:
#               c(MONparameters,IterationNumberAtTermination,
ConvergenceIndicator)
#       
#               "MONparameters"
#                                               PARAMETER VECTOR OF THE FORM
(p1,...pN,u1,...uN,s1,...,sN)
#                                               WHERE (pI,uI,sI) ARE MIXTURE
PROPORTION, MEAN, AND
#                                               STANDARD DEVIATION OF NORMAL
I IN THE MIXTURE.
#
#               "IterationNumberAtTermination"
#                                               ITERATION AT EM TERMINATION
#
#               "ConvergenceIndicator"
#                                               ConvergenceIndicator=0 
#                                                       INDICATES ALGORITHM
DID NOT CONVERGE.  POSSIBLE CAUSES:
#                                                       1) NEAR DIVISION BY
ZERO IN HAMILTON EQNS,
#                                                       2) ST.DEV. OF ONE
COMPONENT NORMAL WAS ESSENTIALLY
#                                                               EQUAL TO
ZERO - I.E., A SINGULARITY OCCURRED)
#                                                       3) MAXIMUM NUMBER OF
ITERATIONS WAS REACHED
#
#                                               ConvergenceIndicator=1
#                                                       INDICATES ALGORITHM
DID CONVERGE - SEQUENTIAL CHANGES
#                                                       IN EACH MON
PARAMETER ACROSS ITERATIONS WERE ALL LESS
#                                                       THAN EMprecis IN
RELATIVE CHANGE. 
#
EMmon<-function(InitialMONparams,InputData,MaxNumEMiterations=100,EMprecis=1
e-005,NumNormals)
{
        ###### INPUT ERROR CHECKING
###########################################
        #
        if(length(dim(Data))>1)
        {
                stop("EMmon FUNCTION WILL TERMINATE - IT REQUIRES A SINGLE
VECTOR
                                OF DATA AS INPUT")
        }
        if(any(is.na(Data)))
        {
                stop("EMmon FUNCTION WILL TERMINATE - IT DOES NOT ALLOW
MISSING VALUES")
        }
        #
        ###### END OF INPUT ERROR CHECKING
#####################################

        ###### HARD CODED PARAMETERS
###########################################
        #
        # FOLLOWING IS USED BELOW TO AVOID A DIVISION BY ZERO.  THIS 
        # NUMBER MinUnconditDensity IS COMPARED AGAINST DENSITY AT EACH
POINT.
        # MinUnconditDensity IS INVERSELY PROPORTIONAL TO STDEV OF DATA
BECAUSE
        # THE SCALE OF THE DENSITY GOES TO ZERO AS STDEVIATION OF DATA
INCREASES
        # PAST UNITY, BUT SCALE OF DENSITY GOES TO 0.39 AS STDEV GOES TO
ZERO.  
        MinUnconditDensity<-(0.00001/(max(1,sqrt(var(InputData)))))
        
        # LOG-LIKELIHOOD OF MIXTURE OF NORMALS BECOMES UNBOUNDED AS ONE
COMPONENT
        # NORMAL STDEV GOES TO ZERO, IN SOME CASES.  SO, THE FOLLOWING IS A
LOWER
        # BOUND FOR THE VALUE OF EACH STANDARD DEVIATION OF EACH COMPONENT
NORMAL
        SingularityStDev<-(sqrt(var(InputData))/50)
        #
        ###### END OF HARD CODED PARAMETERS
####################################
        

        
        # FOLLOWING GIVES 3 PARAMETERS FOR EACH NORMAL: (p,mean,variance)
        NumMixtureParams<-(3*NumNormals) 
        
        # FOLLOWING IS MATRIX OF CONDITIONAL PROBABILITIES OF EACH
OBSERVATION
        # ...BEING IN EACH OF THE NumNormals STATES 
        ObsnProbs<-matrix(NA,nrow=length(InputData),ncol=NumNormals) 
        
        # VECTORS THAT HOLD PARAMETER ESTIMATES FOR MIXTURE OF NORMALS:
        uhat<-numeric(NumNormals) # MEANS
        shat<-numeric(NumNormals) # VARIANCES (VERIFY)
        phat<-numeric(NumNormals) # MIXTURE PROPORTIONS
        
        # FUTURE IMPROVE - MODIFY INPUT SO THAT VECTOR OF P'S IS FROM
1-NumNormals. WHEN
        # ...DOING THIS, MUST ALSO MODIFY GLOBAL FUNCTION BELOW AT SAME
TIME...
        # ...TO GUARANTEE COMPATIBILITY - GOT IT WRONG ON FIRST TRY.  THEN
        # ...DROP VARIABLE NAME 'x' AND USE SOMETHING MORE DESCRIPTIVE. 
        
        # FOLLOWING IS A VECTOR TO HOLD ALL OF THE 3*NumNormals MIXTURE
PARAMETERS 
        x<-numeric(NumMixtureParams)
        Pn<-(1-(sum(InitialMONparams[1:(NumNormals-1)])))
        
x<-c(InitialMONparams[1:(NumNormals-1)],Pn,InitialMONparams[NumNormals:lengt
h(InitialMONparams)])  # new parameter vector
        
        
        nocon<-x # VALUE OF PARAMETERS RETURNED IF CONVERGENCE IS NOT
REACHED
                                #  ...(WHY NOT JUST RETURN x AT WHATEVER
VALUE IT IS AT...
                                # ...WHEN NO-CONVERG. OCCURS??). 
        
        EMconverged<-0          # EMconverged IS SET TO 1 IF/WHEN
CONVERGENCE IS REACHED.  
        z<-numeric(NumMixtureParams)
        CON<-numeric(NumMixtureParams+2) # VALUE OF PARAMETERS RETURNED IF
CONVERGENCE OCCURS
        
        i<-0                    
        while(i<=MaxNumEMiterations && EMconverged==0)
        {
                i<-i+1
                                
                # CALCULATE UNCONDITIONAL DENSITY OF EACH DATA POINT IN
InputData(t). 
                #       NOTE THAT "denom" THAT RESULTS IS DENOMINATOR OF
22.3.7 IN 
                #       HAMILTON (P.688), WHICH CORRESPONDS TO RESULTS OF
22.3.5 IN
                #       HAMILTON (P.686).
                denom<-rep(0,length(InputData))
                for(j in 1:NumNormals)
                {       
        
denom<-denom+(x[j]*dnorm(InputData,x[j+NumNormals],x[j+2*NumNormals]))
                } 

                # DENOM[j]<MinUnconditDensity MEANS WE ARE CLOSE TO DIVISION
BY ZERO,
                # ...SO TERMINATE
                # OLD VERSION - if(any(denom==0))
                if(any(denom<MinUnconditDensity))       
                {
                        CON<-c(nocon,i,0) 
                        return(CON)
                }
                # "return" STATEMENT HERE CAUSES FUNCTION TO TERMINATE AT
THIS POINT.  
                # WHEN USING THIS FUNCTION IN A GLOBAL OPTIMIZATION
FRAMEWORK, THE 
                # ...IDEA WOULD BE TO TRY AGAIN WITH A NEW PARAMETER VECTOR.

                
                
                # EQUATIONS 22.3.7-22.3.10 IN HAMILTON, P.688.

                for(j in 1:NumNormals)
                {
        
ObsnProbs[,j]<-(x[j]*dnorm(InputData,x[j+NumNormals],x[j+2*NumNormals]))/den
om
        
uhat[j]<-(sum(InputData*ObsnProbs[,j]))/sum(ObsnProbs[,j])
        
shat[j]<-sum(((InputData-x[j+NumNormals])^2)*ObsnProbs[,j])/(sum(ObsnProbs[,
j]))
                        phat[j]<-sum(ObsnProbs[,j])/length(InputData)
                }  

                # CONVERT FROM VARIANCES TO SDEVS
                shat<-sqrt(shat) 
                                
                # FIRST (NumNormals-1) P-HAT ENTRIES DETERMINE NumNormals-TH
ENTRY
                phat[NumNormals]<-1-sum((phat[1:NumNormals-1])) 
                
                # THE FOLLOWING CHECKS TO SEE IF ALGORITHM FOUND A
SINGULARITY
                # IF (SINGULARITY FOUND) THEN (RETURN TWO THINGS:
                #               1) EMconverged OF ZERO INDICATING NO
CONVERGENCE.
                #               2) NUMBER OF ITERATIONS
                
                # SINGULARITY OCCURS AS AN shat APPROACHES ZERO BECAUSE
LOG-LIKELIHOOD...
                # ...BECOMES UNBOUNDED. 
                if(any(shat<SingularityStDev)) 
                {
                        CON<-c(nocon,i,0)
                        return(CON)                     
                }
                
                # CHECK TO SEE IF TERMINATION CRITERIA HAVE BEEN MET
                z<-c(phat,uhat,shat) 
                RelativeError<-abs((z-x)/z) # ABSOLUTE VALUE OF RELATIVE
ERROR
                EMconverged<-ifelse(all(RelativeError<EMprecis),1,0)
                
                # SAVE MON PARAMETERS FOR THE NEXT ITERATION:
                x<-z 
        
                CON<-c(x,i,EMconverged) 
                # CON RETURNS: 
                # c(parameters, iter number at termination, whether or not 
                # ...error criterion was satisfied at termination)

   }
        cat(paste("TERMINAL ITERATION OF EMmon IS ",i," \n",collapse=NULL))
        return(CON) 
        # RETURNS MLE PARAMETERS, NUM.ITERATIONS, AND EMconverged=1 IF
CONVERGED.  
}
#
####### end of FUNCTION EMmon
##################################################

#######  FUNCTION GlobalOptEMmon
#########################################################
#
# FUNCTION:
#               GlobalOptEMmon
#
# PURPOSE:
#               ESTIMATES PARAMETERS FOR A MIXTURE OF N NORMALS FOR A DATA
VECTOR.
#               DIFFERS FROM FUNCTION "EMmon" IN THAT GlobalOptEMmon CALLS
EMmon
#               REPEATEDLY TO FIND THE BEST OVERALL SOLUTION ACROSS ALL SUCH
CALLS.
#               INITIAL CALL USES A PRECHOSEN START SET OF PARAMETERS.
#               SUBSEQUENT ITERATIONS USE RANDOMLY CHOSEN MON PARAMETERS TO
ATTEMPT
#               TO IMPROVE ON THE INITIAL SOLUTION
#
# REFERENCE:
#               SEE HAMILTON, JAMES D.(1994).  TIME SERIES, PP.685-689.
#
# RECOMMENDATION FOR CHOOSING INPUT PARAMETER VALUES:
#               * "MaxNumEMiterations" SHOULD BE CHOSEN SO THAT ALGORITHM
CONVERGES
#                       MOST BUT NOT ALL OF THE TIME.
#
# INPUTS:
#               "InitialMONparams"              
#                                               MIXTURE OF NORMALS (MON)
PARAMETERS.
#                                               THESE MUST BE INPUT IN THE
ORDER
#
InitialMONparams=(p1,p2,..p(N-1),u1,u2,...,uN,s1,s2,..,sN) 
# <FUTURE - CONVERT TO P1-PN INPUT - DO EMmon SIMULATANEOUSLY>
# 
#               "InputData"                             
#                                               A DATA VECTOR
#
#               "MaxNumEMiterations"                    
#                                               MAXIMUM NUMBER OF ITERATIONS
OF THE EM ALGORITHM
#                                               FOR MON TO OBTAIN
CONVERGENCE.  THIS MAXIMUM NUMBER
#                                               IS OVERRIDDEN IF ERROR
TOLERANCE "EMprecis" (NEXT
#                                               ARGUMENT) IS SATISFIED.  
#
#               "EMprecis"      
#                                               PRECISION REQUIRED FOR
CONVERGENCE OF EM ALGORITHM
#
#               "NumNormals"                            
#                                               NUMBER OF NORMALS IN THE
MIXTURE OF NORMALS
#
#               "NumGlobalOptIterations"
#                                               NUMBER OF ITERATIONS
PERFORMED IN THE GLOBAL OPTIMIZATION
#
# OUTPUT:
#
ReturnList<-list(InitialMONresults=InitialSolutionForOutput,BestMONresults=B
estSolutionForOutput)
#               THE PREVIOUS RETURNED RESULT BREAKS DOWN INTO THE FOLLOWING
PARTS.
#               THE FIRST PART CONTAINS EM RESULTS BASED ON THE FIRST
STARTING POINT
#               THE SECOND PART CONTAINS BEST EM RESULTS FOR ALL STARTING
POINTS
#
InitialSolutionForOutput<-list(MONparamEsts=InitialEMsolution,InitialLogLike
lihood=InitialLogLikelihood)
#
BestSolutionForOutput<-list(BestEMsolution=BestEMsolution,MaxLogLikelihood=M
axLogLikelihood)        
#
#               WE EXPLAIN EACH OF THE ELEMENTS IN THIS RETURN VIA THE
FOLLOWING EXAMPLE:
#
# EXAMPLE OUTPUT:
#
# ENTRIES 1-6 ARE (p1,p2,u1,u2,s1,s2) - MIXTURE PARAMETERS
# ENTRY 7 IS FINAL ITERATION NUMBER IN EM ALGORITHM
# ENTRY 8 INDICATES "EM CONVERGED" (1) OR "EM DID NOT CONVERGE" (0)
# $InitialMONresults:
# $InitialMONresults$MONparamEsts:
# [1] 0.50000000 0.50000000 0.08602459 0.08602459 4.64783878 4.64783878
# [7] 2.00000000 1.00000000
#
# THIS IS THE LOG-LIKELIHOOD OF THE TERMINAL ITERATION OF THE INITIAL EM
SOLN
# $InitialMONresults$InitialLogLikelihood:
# [1] -1477.67
#
# ENTRIES HERE - FINAL GLOBALLY OPTIMAL RESULT - HAVE THE SAME
INTERPRETATION
#       THEY DO FOR THE INITIAL RESULT.
# $BestMONresults:
# $BestMONresults$BestEMsolution:
# [1]   0.29296530   0.70703470   0.06702855   0.09389574   1.49952721
# [6]   5.44257297 105.00000000   1.00000000
#
# $BestMONresults$MaxLogLikelihood:
# [1] -1457.235
#
#
GlobalOptEMmon<-function(InitialMONparams,InputData,MaxNumEMiterations,
        
EMprecis,NumNormals,NumGlobalOptIterations)
{
        ###### INPUT ERROR CHECKING
###########################################
        #
        if(length(dim(Data))>1)
        {
                stop("GlobalOptEMmon FUNCTION WILL TERMINATE - IT REQUIRES A
SINGLE VECTOR
                                OF DATA AS INPUT")
        }
        if(any(is.na(Data)))
        {
                stop("GlobalOptEMmon FUNCTION WILL TERMINATE - IT DOES NOT
ALLOW MISSING VALUES")
        }
        #
        ###### END OF INPUT ERROR CHECKING
#####################################

        ###### HARD CODED PARAMETERS
###########################################
        #
        # FOLLOWING DETERMINES MAXIMUM NUMBER OF ITERATIONS ALLOWED FOR 
        # EM ALGORITHM TO CONVERGE IN INITIAL ATTEMPT TO FIND A SOLUTION
        # PRIOR TO GLOBAL OPTIMIZATION STEP
        # 
        NumItersForInitialEMconvergence<-1000
        #
        # THE FOLLOWING ARE USED IN GLOBAL OPTIMIZATION PROCESS.
        # RANDOM PROPORTIONS ARE SAMPLED FROM THIS INTERVAL.
        # RANDOM MEANS OF NORMALS ALSO USE THESE QUANTILES AS BOUNDS
        UnifPerturbLowerBound<-0.001
        UnifPerturbUpperBound<-0.999
        # ...STANDARD DEVIATIONS ARE SAMPLED FROM A UNIFORM DISTRIBUTION,
WITH
        # ...THESE MULTIPLIERS TIMES THE SAMPLE STANDARD DEVIATION AS THE
BOUNDS
        StdevPerturbLowerBound<-(1/20)
        StdevPerturbUpperBound<-30      
        #
        ###### END OF HARD CODED PARAMETERS
####################################

                
        # STEP 1:
        #
        # FIND AN INITIAL LOCALLY OPTIMAL SOLUTION USING EMmon
        
InitialEMsolution<-EMmon(InitialMONparams,InputData,MaxNumEMiterations,EMpre
cis,NumNormals)
        
        # LAST ENTRY OF InitialEMsolution INDICATES CONVERGENCE (1) OR NOT
(0) OF EMmon.
        EMconverged<-InitialEMsolution[length(InitialEMsolution)]  
        

        # STEP 2:
        #
        # IF INITIAL PARAMS DO NOT CONVERGE THEN PERTURB THEM UNTIL
CONVERGENCE
        DataStDev<-sqrt(var(InputData))
        i<-0
        while(i<=NumItersForInitialEMconvergence && EMconverged==0)
        {
                i<-i+1

        
MixtureProportions<-runif(NumNormals,UnifPerturbLowerBound,UnifPerturbUpperB
ound) 
        
MixtureProportions<-MixtureProportions/sum(MixtureProportions)
        
InitialMONparams[1:(NumNormals-1)]<-MixtureProportions[1:(NumNormals-1)]
                                
                # PERTURB THE MEANS:
        
InitialMONparams[NumNormals:(2*NumNormals-1)]<-runif(NumNormals,quantile(Inp
utData,UnifPerturbLowerBound),quantile(InputData,UnifPerturbUpperBound)) 

                # PERTURB THE STDEVS:
                for(j in (2*NumNormals):length(InitialMONparams))
                {                       
        
InitialMONparams[j]<-runif(1,DataStDev*StdevPerturbLowerBound,DataStDev*Stde
vPerturbUpperBound)
                }
                # InitialEMsolution HAS THE FOLLOWING PARTS: 
                # ...c(MONparameters,IterationNumberAtTermination,
ConvergenceIndicator)
        
InitialEMsolution<-EMmon(InitialMONparams,InputData,MaxNumEMiterations,EMpre
cis,NumNormals)
                EMconverged<-InitialEMsolution[length(InitialEMsolution)]
        }
        
        if(EMconverged==0)
        {
                stop("PROGRAM STOPPED BECAUSE INITIAL PARAMETER ESTIMATES
DID NOT CONVERGE.")
        }
        else
        {
                cat("INITIAL EM PARAMETER ESTIMATES FOUND.  \n")
        }
                
        # COMPUTE LOG-LIKELIHOOD VALUES OF INITIAL ESTIMATE:    
        denom<-rep(0,length(InputData))
        for(i in 1:NumNormals)
        {
        
denom<-denom+(InitialEMsolution[i]*dnorm(InputData,InitialEMsolution[i+NumNo
rmals],InitialEMsolution[i+2*NumNormals]))
        }
        InitialLogLikelihood<-sum(log(denom))
        MaxLogLikelihood<-InitialLogLikelihood  
        
        # list of param estimates from inital MOM inputs and its likelihood
value
        # this will be returned with information on global optimization
results
        
        
InitialSolutionForOutput<-list(MONparamEsts=InitialEMsolution,InitialLogLike
lihood=InitialLogLikelihood)
        BestEMsolution<-InitialEMsolution
        # InitialEMsolution HAS THE FOLLOWING PARTS: 
        # ...c(MONparameters,IterationNumberAtTermination,
ConvergenceIndicator)
        
        # STEP 3:
        #
        # GLOBAL OPTIMIZATION - ATTEMPT TO IMPROVE ON INITIAL LOCALLY
OPTIMAL SOLUTION
        for(i in 1:NumGlobalOptIterations)
        {
                cat("\n","GLOBAL OPT. ITER. = ",i, " \n")
                
                tempMONparam<-InitialMONparams          
                
                # RANDOMLY PERTURB THE MIXTURE PROPORTIONS
        
tempMONparam[1:NumNormals]<-runif(NumNormals,UnifPerturbLowerBound,UnifPertu
rbUpperBound) 
        
tempMONparam[1:NumNormals]<-(tempMONparam[1:NumNormals])/sum(tempMONparam[1:
NumNormals])
                
                # RANDOMLY PERTURB THE MEANS
        
tempMONparam[NumNormals:(2*NumNormals-1)]<-runif(NumNormals,quantile(InputDa
ta,UnifPerturbLowerBound),quantile(InputData,UnifPerturbUpperBound))
        
                # RANDOMLY PERTURB THE STANDARD DEVIATIONS
                for(j in (2*NumNormals):length(InitialMONparams))
                {
        
tempMONparam[j]<-runif(1,DataStDev*StdevPerturbLowerBound,DataStDev*StdevPer
turbUpperBound)
                }
                        
                # FIND EMmon SOLUTION GIVEN PERTURBED PARAMETERS AS STARTING
POINTS:
        
CurrentEMresults<-EMmon(tempMONparam,InputData,MaxNumEMiterations,EMprecis,N
umNormals)
                # CurrentEMresults HAS THE FOLLOWING PARTS: 
                # ...c(MONparameters,IterationNumberAtTermination,
ConvergenceIndicator)
                
                # LAST ENTRY IN VECTOR "CurrentEMresults" IS 0 IF EM DID NOT
CONVERGE.
                # SO, IF PERTURBED RESULTS DO NOT CONVERGE THEN GO TO NEXT
TRIAL:
                if(CurrentEMresults[length(CurrentEMresults)]==0)
                {
                        cat(paste("GLOBAL OPT. ITER. ",i, "DID NOT CONVERGE.
\n"),collapse=NULL)
                        next    # SKIP TO NEXT ITERATION OF GLOBAL
OPTIMIZATION.  
                }
                
                # CALCULATE NEW LOG-LIKELIHOOD VALUE FOR ESTIMATED
PARAMETERS
                denom<-rep(0,length(InputData))
           for(k in 1:NumNormals)
                {
        
denom<-denom+(CurrentEMresults[k]*dnorm(InputData,CurrentEMresults[k+NumNorm
als],CurrentEMresults[k+2*NumNormals]))
                }
           EMlogLikelihood<-sum(log(denom))
        
                # IF NEW LIKELIHOOD VALUE IS GREATER THAN PREVIOUS, THEN
GLOBALLY OPTIMAL
                # ...PARAMETER VALUES ARE REPLACED WITH CURRENT PARAMETER
VALUES
                if(EMlogLikelihood>MaxLogLikelihood)
                { 
                        BestEMsolution<-CurrentEMresults
                        MaxLogLikelihood<-EMlogLikelihood
                }
                cat(paste("END OF GLOBAL OPT. ITER. = ",i, "\n"),
collapse=NULL)
                cat(paste("CURRENT LOGLIKELIHOOD = ",EMlogLikelihood, "\n"),
collapse=NULL)
                cat(paste("MAX LOGLIKELIHOOD = ",MaxLogLikelihood, "\n"),
collapse=NULL)
        } 
        # END OF "for(i in 1:NumGlobalOptIterations)"
        
        # RETURN INITIAL SOLUTION AND BEST SOLUTION:
        
BestSolutionForOutput<-list(BestEMsolution=BestEMsolution,MaxLogLikelihood=M
axLogLikelihood)
        
ReturnList<-list(InitialMONresults=InitialSolutionForOutput,BestMONresults=B
estSolutionForOutput)
        return(ReturnList)
}
#
#######  end of FUNCTION GlobalOptEMmon
##################################################

# This function calcultes the conditional probability of state j given y(t)
# Inputs
# params<-(p1,p2,...,pN,u1,u2,...,uN,s1,s2,...,sN)
# Y<-data
# NumNormals<-number of states

StatePs<-function(params,Y,NumNormals)
{       
        x<-params;
        ObsnProbs<-matrix(NA,nrow=length(Y),ncol=NumNormals); #conditional
probability matrix
        denom<-rep(0,length(Y));
        for(i in 1:NumNormals)
        {
        
denom<-denom+(x[i]*dnorm(Y,x[i+NumNormals],x[i+2*NumNormals]))
        } 
        #calculate unconditional prob of each Y(t)
                        
        for(i in 1:NumNormals)
        {
        
ObsnProbs[,i]<-(x[i]*dnorm(Y,x[i+NumNormals],x[i+2*NumNormals]))/denom;
        }
        # calculate p(s(t)=j|y(t))
        
        return(ObsnProbs)
        
}

You have a gam fit, so don't expect glm methods to work.
Although gam fits have been given class
> class(.Last.value)
[1] "gam" "glm" "lm"
that's not right, as it is suppose to guarantee that *any* glm method will
work correctly.  There are similar issues with glm inheriting from lm.

There is no profile method provided for gam, not least because there is no
guarantee that the gam() fitting method finds the mle: it only finds
somewhere close to a fairly flat region, and there can be many local
maxima.

You need more precise version numbers than `6.2' (6.2pl006 is current), but
MASS is no longer maintained for 4.5: we have not run that obselete version
for a long time (2000 is nearly two years old and 6.0 is round the corner,
and each needs considerably different versions).

messages.subject: Re: strange profile likelihood result
messages.body_plain:
If you fit a gam, the estimates are *not* maximum likelihood but maximum
penalized likelihood.  During your updating process the penalty term is also
updated so the likelihood that you calculate need not vary monotonically (as
this is just one term in the objective function).

I suspect this is the cause of your dilemma.  If you want an approximate
answer (probably to the right problem) you might replace s(x2) in our
original problem with a natural spline basis, say ns(x2, df=5) (??) and use
glm() rather than gam() to fit a reasonable approximation to the gam by
genuine maximum likelihood.  You should then be able to use profile.glm
(from the MASS library) to examine your likelihood profile and obtain your
confidence interval.

Bill Venables.

On Mon, 11 Jun 2001, George W. Gilchrist wrote:

> Does anyone have a function for drawing latitude and longitude lines on a
> map produced with Splus' map function? If not, does anyone have a clue about
> how to draw such lines? I have tried several ideas without success. Thanks.

Below is one that I hacked together a while ago, no guarentees, but it
seems to work.  Just make sure that you call map() with a projection (the
default does not always create an object that is needed by my function)

> library(maps)
> map('state',plot=F)$range
[1] -124.68134  -67.00742   25.12993   49.38323
> map('state', projection='sinu')
> map.grid( seq(-125, -65, by=10), seq(25,50,by=5) )
> map('state', projection='sinu',xlim=c(-155,-35))
> map.grid( seq(-125, -65, by=10), seq(25,50,by=5),
+ xlim=c(-130,-60), ylim=c(22,53), offset=-0.05 )
> map.grid( seq(-125, -65, by=10), seq(25,50,by=5),
+ xlim=c(-130,-60), ylim=c(22,53), offset=-0.5 )

hope this helps,

map.grid <- function(long, lat, res=40, xlim=range(long), ylim=range(lat), 
                     labels=T, offset=0.05, lty=2,col=1,
                     projection = .Last.projection$projection, 
                     parameters = .Last.projection$parameters, 
                     orientation = .Last.projection$orientation) {

# Function to draw grid lines on maps from the maps library
# Written by Greg Snow, gls at byu.edu
        
        #  verticle
        
        x1 <- rep( long, each=res+1 )
        x1[ seq(along=long)*(res + 1) ] <- NA
        
        y1 <- rep( c(seq(ylim[1],ylim[2], length=res),NA), length(long) )
        
        #  Horizontal
        
        y2 <- rep( lat, each=res+1 )
        y2[ seq(along=lat)*(res+1) ] <- NA
        
        x2 <- rep( c(seq(xlim[1],xlim[2], length=res),NA), length(lat) )
        
        
        # draw lines
        
        lines( mapproject(x1,y1,projection, parameters, orientation), lty=lty, 
col=col )
        lines( mapproject(x2,y2,projection, parameters, orientation), lty=lty, 
col=col )

        if(labels){
                text( mapproject( c(long,long), rep(ylim, each=length(long))+
                                   
rep(c(-1,1),each=length(long))*offset*diff(ylim), 
                                  projection, parameters, orientation),
                      as.character(c(long,long)) )
                text( mapproject( rep(xlim, each=length(lat))+
                                   
rep(c(-1,1),each=length(lat))*offset*diff(xlim), c(lat,lat), 
                                  projection, parameters, orientation),
                      labels=as.character(c(lat,lat)) )

        }
                
invisible(NULL) 
}

On Mon, 11 Jun 2001, George W. Gilchrist wrote:

> Does anyone have a function for drawing latitude and longitude lines on a
> map produced with Splus' map function? If not, does anyone have a clue about
> how to draw such lines? I have tried several ideas without success. Thanks.

Here is a function I wrote called makegraticule.f, with an example below
it along with a function for Projecting the gratiule into an Albers Equal
Area Conic Projection.

makegraticule.f <- function(startlong = -40, endlong = -140, startlat = 0,
incrementlong = -10, increment = 10)
{
        grat <- vector("numeric")
        xn <- seq(startlong, endlong, incrementlong)
        nreps <- length(xn)
        for(i in 1:nreps) {
                lats <- seq(startlat, 90, increment)
                longs <- rep(startlong, length(lats))
                grat <- rbind(grat, cbind(longs, lats), c(NA, NA))
                startlong <- startlong - increment
        }
        nreps <- length(seq(startlat, 90, increment))
        for(i in 1:nreps) {
                longs <- xn
                lats <- rep(startlat, length(longs))
                grat <- rbind(grat, cbind(longs, lats), c(NA, NA))
                startlat <- startlat + increment
        }
        grat
}

EXAMPLE:

        gratic <- makegraticule.f(startlong = -20, endlong = -180,
startlat=0,)

gratic<-makegraticule.f(startlong = -40, endlong = -140, startlat = 0,
incrementlong = -10, increment = 10)

Makes a graticule in LONG/LAT from 40W to 140W and with latitudes rangeing
from 0 to 90 N by 10 degrees longitude and 10 degrees latitude. 
        

You may be interested in this one as well which is the forward solution
for Albers Equal Area Conic Projection which allows you to set specific
origin and standardlines, example:

        #project lines to new coordinate system using albers.mat.f
        gratic <- albers.mat.f(gratic, c(-100, 80), c(40, 80))  #

Projectes the Graticule into Albers Equal Area Conic Projection with an
origin of 100 W and 80 N with Standard lines at 40 and 80 N.  An example
of the map output in S+ using this can be seen at:

http://www.uottawa.ca/academic/arts/geographie/lpcweb/PCSPdata/P1974.JPG

Or just try:

plot(albers.mat.f(makegraticule.f(), c(-100, 80), c(40, 80)),type="n")
lines(albers.mat.f(makegraticule.f(), c(-100, 80), c(40, 80)))
for a quick look.

albers.mat.f <- function(xy, origin = c(0, 0), stdlns = c(0, 0))
{
#R - Earth Radius
#phi1 - Lat; Stdln 1
#phi2 - Lat; Stdln 2
#phi0 - Lat; Origin
#lambda0 - Lon; Origin
#xy - c(phi,lambda); point to be projected
#C = (cos(phi1))^2+2nsin(phi1)
#n=(sin(phi1)+sin(phi2))/2
#theta = n(lambda-lambda0)
#p = (R(C-2n sin(phi))^.5)/n
#pnot = (R(C-2n sin (phi0))^.5)/n
#x = p sin(theta)
#y = pnot - p cos(theta)
        xy <- as.matrix(xy)
        dimnames(xy) <- list(NULL, c("x", "y")) #dimnames(xy) <- NULL
        xy <- (xy * pi)/180
        R <- 6378 * 1000
        phi1 <- (stdlns[1] * pi)/180
        phi2 <- (stdlns[2] * pi)/180
        phi0 <- (origin[2] * pi)/180
        lambda0 <- (origin[1] * pi)/180 #
############
        n <- (sin(phi1) + sin(phi2))/2
        twon <- 2 * n
        C <- ((cos(phi1))^2 + 2 * n * sin(phi1))
        theta <- n * (xy[, 1] - lambda0)
        xy[, 1] <- ((R * (C - twon * sin(xy[, 2]))^0.5)/n) * sin(theta)
        xy[, 2] <- ((R * (C - twon * sin(phi0))^0.5)/n) - ((R * (C - 2 * n
* sin(xy[, 
                2]))^0.5)/n) * cos(theta)
        xy
}

messages.subject: Acknowledgments: testing for ANOVA
messages.body_plain:
Thanks to Steve McKinney, Dennis Murphy, Andrew Sinclair, Andy Liaw,
Mat Souckup and Greg Arnold for sharing their insight and expertise
regarding my ANOVA question.

I found particularly useful Dennis' references to the books of Searle
and previous S-news threads, and the connections to "Type I vs III
sums of squares".

Best,

        Florin

On Thu, 24 May 2001, Florin Vaida wrote:

> Dear S-newsers,
> 
> I have a straightforward ANOVA question.
> 
> Consider a 2-way ANOVA model, such as
> 
> fit.2way <- lm(y ~ treatment + nnrti, data=actg)
> 
> Running the anova() command I get:
> fv>  anova(fit.2way)
> Analysis of Variance Table
> Terms added sequentially (first to last)
>            Df Sum of Sq  Mean Sq  F Value      Pr(F) 
> treatment   3    6.6470  2.21566  2.37301 0.06971484
> nnrti       1   50.1968 50.19681 53.76172 0.00000000
> Residuals 435  406.1555  0.93369                    
> 
> Question:  What is the interpretation of the "treatment" test?
> 
> For the longest time I thought that this is exactly the test
> for the "treatment" factor from the 1-way ANOVA model (i.e., ignoring the 
> second factor, "nnrti"), but it is not:
> 
> fv>  fit.1way ~ lm(y ~ nnrti, data=actg)
> fv>  anova(fit.1way)
> Analysis of Variance Table
> Terms added sequentially (first to last)
>            Df Sum of Sq  Mean Sq  F Value      Pr(F) 
> treatment   3    6.6470 2.215661 2.116848 0.09738108
> Residuals 436  456.3523 1.046680                    
> 
> (The 1-way ANOVA and 2-way ANOVA yield same treatment SS, but the F-tests
> have different residual SS and Df).
> 
> Also, in general this is not the same as the "standard" test for the
> "treatment" factor, after controlling for "nnrti", unless the design
> is balanced.
> 
> Thanks for the insights,
> 
>       Florin
> 
> 
> 
> 
> 
>

>

> Florin Vaida
> Assist Prof, Dept of Biostatistics
> Harvard School of Public Health

Florin Vaida

    x   y

              x             y

One obvious solution to my problem is to save the SAS datasets with 8 bytes
per field.  However, I have a large amount of data in SAS (both in terms of

per numeric field, so I'd like to avoid this path if possible.

Any suggestions?

Matt Van Vlack

messages.subject: Memory and batch issues
messages.body_plain:
I would appreciate any advice my on the following issues.

I am using S+2000 R2 on NT4 with 512MB RAM.

I am carrying out simulations on the company level data. My datasets
typically have 150,000-250,000 rows and 70 columns. I need to carry the
simulations out over several combinations of parameters and resorted to
using S-Plus in Batch mode to carry this out. I do this by right clicking on
the S-Plus icon and adding /BATCH job.txt after S-Plus in the Target field.
I resorted to BATCH mode when S-Plus warned of a lack of virtual memory
whewn I tried to run the same job at the command line. My job.txt file looks
something like

jj.perf<-f.simulation(df, "first set of parameters")
print(jj.perf)
.
.
.
jj.perf<-f.simulation(df, "i th set of parameters")
print(jj.perf)

where df is the dataframe. For the larger datasets each simulation runs in 2
and a half minutes at the command line but the average simulation (all
identical in operation except for the parameter set) when I submit a hundred
or so parameter sets in a job file takes about 9 minutes. Very quickly there
is a lot of hard drive activity as obviously a large amount of paging is
taking place. Monitoring Windows memory using Task Manager shows me the
available Physical Memory is very low.

In Appendix C of Venables and Ripley's S Programming, batching is described
using sqpe. I have tried to use this to batch jobs but have not been
successful. Is this a superior way to carry out batching and if so can
anyone give some advice on how they work this under Windows?

Given the amount of RAM I have I assume that some of my problem resides in
my coding. What is the best way to track down the area of code that is
memory inefficient. I could dos.time the sub functions in f.simulation to
see where performance was degrading. Would it make sense to place
mem.tally.report in strategic places in the code or use storage.summary
(described in the S-Plus Programmers manual)? I have never been sure where
the correct place to put mem.tally.report commands when dealing with sub
functions?

On a specific point, when dealing with a large dataframe (say Df) and a
function with alters a column does it make any difference whether the
function is constructed so that the call is either
Df$column<-f.alter.column(Df)
Or
Df<-f.alter.column(Df)? Any tips and tricks on how to allow sub functions to
release memory would really be appreciated.

Sincerest thanks in advance
Glenn Treacy

messages.body_plain:
At 02:18 PM 06/14/01 -0400, Park, Kyong H Mr. SBCCOM wrote:
> Dear S+ users, I have a co-worker who wants to know  how to compute the
> error function erf(x) for x>6 . He checked Matlab and Mathematica
> (erf(6)=1). He is not satisfied with the accuracy which is based on
> Chebychev polinom. I appreciate your help.
>
> Kyong        US Army
>
>
>
> ---------------------------------------------------------------------
> This message was distributed by s-news at lists.biostat.wustl.edu.  To
> unsubscribe send e-mail to s-news-request at lists.biostat.wustl.edu with
> the BODY of the message:  unsubscribe s-news

In Mathematica, use the N function with a specified number of decimal 
digits.  E.g.

N[Erf[10],100]

0.9999999999999999999999999999999999999999999979115124162374552429992137050422\
1138843918188067883627299

S-PLUS only has 16 digits of precision, so erf(6) rounds to 1, but you can 
compute the difference between 1 and the erf by:

erfdif <- function(x) {2*pnorm(-x*sqrt(2))}
> erfdif(6)
[1] 2.151974e-017

messages.subject: Re: stop error interruptions
messages.body_plain:
On Thu, 14 Jun 2001, Gunter, Bert wrote:

> I am replying to the list because I am not sure whether the advice I am
> dispensing is correct. So I hope others will correct me if this is off the
> wall. In any case, it is most certainly dangerous (infinite loops can easily
> occur). The advice is: try using the restart() function.

It's right, but it safer is use the try() function, which is a wrapper
for restart().  try() exists in S-PLUS 2000, but unfortunately not in its
the help pages.  Page 48 of `S Programming' may help.

Something like

for(i in 1:nsim) {
    x[i] <- <null value>
    try({
      fit <- nls( <snipped> )
      lines( <snipped> )
      x[i] <- <snipped>
    })
}

options(error=NULL) removes the error action (dump.calls by default)
but the expression which fails, here for(), will still be aborted.

--

messages.subject: Re: Passing data frame by pointer
messages.body_plain:
> Is there a
> way to write a function which would just work on the given data frame,
> without making a copy of it?  We are using Splus2000, but can switch to
> Splus6 (pr3) if there is large advantage.

Switching to S-PLUS 6 would indeed be a large advantage.  In S version 4,
function calls are implementationally call-by-reference (though still
semantically call-by-value).  The upshot of this is that if you pass a large
object to a function, that object is not copied in memory unless the object
is modified.  This is ideal for passing around large blocks of data.

More details in the S-PLUS 6 white paper at
http://www.insightful.com/products/splus/about6.html.

# David Smith

messages.subject: Summary: stop error interruptions
messages.body_plain:
Thanks to Leonid Gibiansky, David Smith, Tim Hesterberg, Steven C. Wofsy,
Bert Gunter, Robert Balshaw, Brian D. Ripley, and Trevor Thompson for
responding to my request for help (see my original posting at the end of
this message).

Most people recommended I use try(), an undocumented S-PLUS function.
Brian Ripley was the only person to give an example of how to use the
function, and it did the trick for me (see sample code below).  He also
referred me to page 48 of 'S Programming'.

for(i in 1:nsim) {
    try({
    fit <- nls( <snipped> )
    lines( <snipped> )
    x[i] <- <snipped>
    })
    }

Other suggestions, that I did not pursue, were to:

1. Use the function on.exit() as part of my for() loop.
2. Use the function restart().  (Noted as dangerous.)
3. Adjust nls() maximum iterations and convergence criteria.

Thanks again for the help.

JVA

messages.body_plain:
Hi Jean,

ran into the same problem numerous times, very annoying.  A maybe dangerous
solution is changing the existing nls function.  There is a section in it
that goes like (Splus 3.3 version).

...
        if(z$control[5])
                stop(switch(as.integer(z$control[5]),
                        "step factor reduced below minimum",
                        "maximum number of iterations exceeded",
                        "singular gradient matrix",
                        "singular design matrix",
                        "singular gradient matrix"))
        nls.out <- list(parameters = z$parameters, formula = .expr, call =
match.call(), residuals = z$outmat[, 1])
        if(algorithm == "plinear") {

        <snipped>

        nls.out$trace <- get("trace.mat", frame = 1)[1:get("last.iteration", 
frame
= 1),  ]

      nls.out
}

The stop(..) makes the nls fail. I changed it to read

...
     if(z$control[5])
     {  # added the {

# changed stop to warning
                warning(switch(as.integer(z$control[5]),
                        "step factor reduced below minimum",
                        "maximum number of iterations exceeded",
                        "singular gradient matrix",
                        "singular design matrix",
                        "singular gradient matrix"))

#added the following two line to give NA as fitted parameters and provide
the nls.out object for later
            for(i in 1:length(z$parameters)) z$parameters[i] <- NA
            nls.out <- list(parameters = z$parameters, formula = .expr, call
= match.call(), residuals = z$outmat[, 1])

     } else { # added this

      nls.out <- list(parameters = z$parameters, formula = .expr, call =
match.call(), residuals = z$outmat[, 1])
        if(algorithm == "plinear") {

        <snipped>

        nls.out$trace <- get("trace.mat", frame = 1)[1:get("last.iteration", 
frame
= 1),  ]

     }  # added this

     nls.out
}

If you need the source code for your existing nls do a
dump("nls",file="clipboard") and paste into your
favorite text editor. I am not quite sure if the Splus2000 has a much
different nls code.

Change at your own risk and save the original nls first before you try
around.
nls.orig <- nls

Cheers
Peter

messages.subject: Collated responses to "dll.load problem"
messages.body_plain:
Thanks to all the S-users who helped me conquer the folowing problem. I am 
particularly indebted to Matt Calder, who even supplied me with a sample 
code of using the FORTRAN/C interface.

Using DUMPBIN helped (as I could see that my symbol was not loaded) and 
Pierre Duchese's (and Matt) information on setting up the *.def file.

#######

I am trying to load a "dll" in S-Plus 2000. I compiled the my code using 
Compaq Visual Fortran 6, and now I am unable to use the code in S.

The name of my SUBROUTINE in Fortran  is "bmlogit", and the statement I use 
is given below, which the result I get.

dll.load("c:\\data\\fortran\\blogit.dll", symbol ="bmlogit_")

Warning messages:

Warning in dll.load("c:\\data\\fortran\\blogit.dll", symbol = : Unable to 
find entry 'bmlogit_' in DLL 'c:\data\fortran\blogit.dll'

[1] 1

Thanks in advance for your help.

Vumani Dlamini
#######
Response from, Matt Calder

Anyway, I can probably help you with your problem. The problem is that

the symbols generated for functions by the compiler are not necessarily the 
sameas those you specified in your code. In particular Fortran will often 
capitalizethe name (ie. BMLOGIT), and Microsoft compilers will often append 
a number that indicates the size in bytes of the arguments (eg. BMLOGIT@16, 
if bmlogit takes four arguments (typically Fortran passes by reference and 
pointers are 4 bytes on PC's)).

In order to find out what your compiler is calling your function you can use 
the File Explorer in Windows (not Internet Explorer). Open the directory 
containing your file and right click it, select 'Quick-view' from the menu, 
this will list a lot of information including the symbol names defined in 
the dll.

(You might be able to find free software on the internet that does this too, 
the name pview comes to mind). A common problem people have is that the dll 
does not export their symbol at all, if you do not see the bmlogit symbol 
referenced at all doing the above, let me know and I'll help you with 
exporting.

#######
Response from, "pierre duchesne" <pierre.duchesne at hec.ca>

Exactly what I m using; use something similar to
dll.load("d:\\Programmation\\ANALYS~1\\Spectre.dll", c("XPGRAM",
"LISTWOUT","SPECDAN") )

Also, maybe you have the same problem that me at the very beginning. in your
fortran code, do not forget to do a DLLEXPORT:

# --- Example ---
subroutine myacf(n,serie,acf)
!dec$ attributes dllexport :: myacf

(code)

return
end
# --- end of example ---

#######
Response from, Prof Brian Ripley <ripley at stats.ox.ac.uk>

The problem seems clearly stated to me!  Use a utility to find out what(if 
any) sysmbols your dll exports.  (E.g. pedump or dumpbin.)

Guesses:

1) You forgot to set up any exports via a .def file.
2) you have set flags which mean that the exported symbol is not
what you think it is.

The first is pretty common ....

######
Response from, "Michael Conklin" <mconklin at customresearch.com>

I believe your symbol should be bmlogit=_bmlogit@4*numparams  for
example if you pass 8 parameters to bmlogit then the symbol would be
symbols=list(bmlogit=_BMLOGIT@32)

By the way - one thing I really like about the candidate release of version 
6 is that all the symbols are loaded automatically. This way if I change my 
subroutine (for example to send more parameters to it) I only have to change 
my S function that calls the subroutine instead of

having to also change the dll.load function in my .first routine.

messages.subject: summary fitting gamma
messages.body_plain:
Dear All:
I would like to express my gratitude to Thomas Yee, James Stapleton, Tim 
Hesterberg,
John Gavin and Greg Snow for the responses to my request on fitting gamma 
ditribution.

Below is the code which I've wrote myself based on the article in the 
encyclopedia of biostatistics 

function(x )
{
#gam.apprxFIT
#fitting parameters shape(k) and rate (1/theta) in gamma distribution
#method is taken from the encyclopedia of biostatistics: gamma distibution, 
page 292

        n <- length(x)
        arith.mean <- mean(x)
        geom.mean <- exp(sum(log(x))/n)
        M <- log(arith.mean/geom.mean)
        if(M >= 0 & M <= 0.5772) {
                est.shape <- (0.5000876 + 0.1648852 * M - 0.0544276 * M^2)/M
        }
        if(M >= 0.5772 & M <= 17) {
                num <- 8.898919 + 9.05995 * M + 0.9775373 * M^2
                den <- M * (17.79728 + 11.968477 * M + M^2)
                est.shape <- num/den
        }
        if(M > 17)
                est.shape <- 1/M
        est.rate <- est.shape/arith.mean
        list(est.shape = est.shape, est.rate = est.rate)
} 

I compared this simple solution with other codes and found the best agreement 
with the John Gavin's code.
Other solutions were also very good.

Again, thank you very much for your help

Xao Ping
R&R Pharmakinetics
Taiwan
